title: 000 Introduction
text:
000 Introduction

(*
 
Theodoric E Stier
theodoric.stier@gmail.com
April 2025

This is an interactive theorem prover based on
first order logic. It is intended to provide to
set theoretic foundations a fraction of the utility
that prevailing proof systems provide to type theoretic
foundations.

There are only a few top-level directives which
introduce propositions and proofs. There are also
only a few proof directives which control the introduction
and closing of hypotheses and goals. The directives
together manipulate two datatypes called *propositions*
and *proofs*. Propositions may or may not be proven,
and a proof's type is the proposition that it proves.

There's no `typeof` or pattern-matching for proofs.

The first line of a file is not interpreted. The
file organizer uses it as the name of the file.
It sorts files alphabetically by name.

*)

title: 010 Propositions
text:
010 Propositions

(*

Propositions are intended for interpretation as
mathematical statements. When so, the proofs supported
by this system correspond to robust and detailed
mathematical proofs of the same statements.

Propositions are the types of proofs, and, as such,
we need ways of combining propositions to to create
*compound propositions*.

First, any identifier, such as `true`, is a proposition.

Given two propositions such as `false` and `true`,
we say `true → false` is also a proposition called
an "arrow" or "implication". You may also type
`->` instead of `→`.

Given two propositions such as `not` and `x` we
say `not x` is also a proposition called an "application".

Given a proposition such as `x → x` with free variable
`x` we say `∀x.x → x` is also a proposition called a
"universal quantification" or just "universal".
You may also type `\` instead of `∀`.

Another similar "quantifier" is `∃`. Such a proposition
`∃x.not x` is called an "existential quantification"
or just "existential". You may also type `/` instead
of `∃`.

Quantifiers with multiple identifiers such as `∀a b.`
are syntax sugar for nested quantifiers such as
`∀a.∀b.`.

Parentheses are required in various places.

A nullary quantifier such as `∀.` can act like
a left parenthesis with an automatic right parenthesis.

We generally require propositions to be *closed*
everywhere, meaning every variable is either declared
globally or bound by some universally quantified
enclosing proposition. E.g. at this point referring
to the proposition `∀a.a → foo` would cause an
error because `foo` is free and not declared globally.

There is a caveat to quantification and application
that we will now discuss. In the term `∀f.f x`,
the occurrence of `f` is not bound by the universal
quantifier because it is in *predicate position*
(the lhs of an application). This prohibition enforces
first order quantification so that we can model
first order logic. No term is permitted to contain
a quantifier or implication in predicate position.

For example, you may uncomment the following line
to see an error that may be reported in relation
to this.

*)

-- axiom not_first_order (∀f x.f x)

(*

Now that we have the ability to construct compound
propositions, we can talk about the `axiom` and
`theorem` directives.

*)

title: 020 Directives and Proving
text:
020 Directives and Proving

(*

One of the essential properties of this system
is the ability to encode and verify proofs.

Use the `theorem` directive to name and state a
provable proposition and begin the sequence of
proof steps. State its name on the same line, then
its proposition. The proof steps must end with
`qed` (to exit theorem mode).

Without declaring any variables or axioms, the
inference rules allow us to prove the following:

"For all `a`, `a` implies `a`."

*)

theorem (implication reflexive)

(∀a.a → a)

(*

(proof steps continue below)

At face value, a → a aligns with intuition. If
something is true, then it is true.

The proof steps proceed by introducing proposition
`a` and evidence `ha` for `a`. `a` and `ha` are
consequently listed in the hypotheses of the active
goal. The last step provides `ha` to close the
goal.

*)

intro a ha
apply ha
qed

(*

While writing the proof, the output window in the
simulator will display the current goals. Each
goal consists of its proposition and a collection
of hypotheses. For example, when we have the following
proof steps:

intro a ha
qed

The output window will display the following goal.

a
ha : a
⊢ a

When all goals are closed, the output window will
display "👍" to indicate the approval of the
sacred boar at the center of the world.

Proofs can use previous theorems.

*)

theorem (right of two)

(∀a b.a → b → b)

(*

Given two propositions, we can conclude the second.
This one is a trivial extension of
`implication reflexive` because the goal
quickly becomes `b → b`.

Here, `apply (implication reflexive) b` specializes
`implication reflexive` for `b` then closes the goal.

*)

intro a b ha
apply (implication reflexive) b
qed

(*

You may have questions about how the proof
directives `intro` and `apply` work. Nothing too
complicated is going on here. `intro` breaks down
universal and arrow goal propositions by adding
propositions and evidence to the hypotheses.

E.g. Say we have the following goal

a
⊢ ∀b.a → b → b

The directive `intro z` will add proposition `z` to
the hypotheses and specialize the goal by manner
of substitution (possibly renaming quantifiers).

a z
⊢ a → z → z

The directive `intro ha` will then add evidence
`ha` of `a` to the hypotheses and reduce the goal.

a z
ha : a
⊢ z → z

You can pile up introductions like `intro z ha`.

`apply` takes a proof and any number of specializations
(for universal proofs) or motives (for arrow proofs),
applies them, then convert antecdents to new goals
until the goal proposition matches.

We can use it to fully close goals or partially
close goals by adding more goals.

Let's not miss `left of two` before we move on.

*)

theorem (left of two)

(∀a b.a → b → a)

(*

Given two propositions, we can conclude the first.
We'll use this for breaking down conjunctions soon.

*)

intro a b ha hb
apply ha
qed

(*

Just a few more implication theorems, then we can end
the chapter.

*)

theorem (implication transitive)

(∀a b c.(a → b) → (b → c) → a → c)

(*

I've said in the past that if we can convert
trees to sticks and sticks to mulch then we
can convert trees to mulch.

*)

intro a b c hab hbc ha
apply hbc
apply hab ha
qed

theorem (implication swap)

(∀a b c.(a → b → c) → b → a → c)

(*

This is functionally equivalent to the statement that
we can switch the first two operands of a function.

Used in `reverse conjunction introduction` to swap
the antecedents.

*)

intro a b c habc hb ha
apply habc ha hb
qed

title: 030 True, False, Negation
text:
030 True, False, Negation

(*

`declare` is another directive which introduces the
propositions listed on the line after it. These
propositions are just names. They function as atoms.

For example, the following `declare` directive
introduces three logical connectives for global
use in later directives.

*)

declare true false not

(*

They don't have any definition yet. We need to use
the `axiom` directive to introduce rules about these
propositions.

`axiom` is a directive like `theorem` but which
requires no proof (or `qed`).

*)

axiom (true introduction)

true

(*

Definition of true.

Almost completely useless. Almost. Nearly everything
involving this can be more simply stated without it.
Sometimes we use it as a base case for fold-like
things. That's about it.

*)

axiom (false elimination)

(false → ∀a.a)

(*

Negation in intuitionistic logic has a special
interpretation. When we write "not A" (¬A), we
are actually saying A implies false ⊥.

More formally: A → ⊥

This is a crucial difference from classical
logic, as we don't assume that ¬¬A implies A.

False and negation relate to absurdity and explosion.
False is defined to imply something impossible
A negation can be used to obtain false from a
contradiction, and false can be used to obtain anything.

Nominally, "For all `a`, `a`." is a false statement
which could be concluded from any other false statement,
but it's also good enough to view it as a rule
for constructing anything.

*)

axiom (negation introduction)

(∀a.(a → false) → not a)

(*

If we wish to prove `not a` then all we must
do is use `a` to show `false`.

*)

axiom (negation elimination)

(∀a.not a → a → false)

(*

If we have `not a` then we also may have that `a`
implies `false`.

In general, we need both introduction and elimination
rules in order to establish equivalence.

Two rare exceptions are that we don't need intro
rule `(∀a.a) → false` or elimination rule
`true → <something true>` because
(a) they're provable anyway and
(b) we'll never use them once in practice

Here are your basic negation theorems.

*)

theorem (non false)

(not false)

(*

This is just `implication reflexive` for false once the
definition of `not` is introduced.

*)

apply (negation introduction) false
apply (implication reflexive) false
qed

theorem (non true)

(not true → false)

intro hnt
apply (negation elimination) true hnt (true introduction)
qed

theorem (of false)

(∀a.false → a)

(*

Often much easier to use than `false elimination`

*)

intro a hf
apply (false elimination) hf a
qed

theorem (false of negation)

(∀a.a → not a → false)

(*

We often have a goal like `not a → false`.
It's easiest to `apply (false of negation) ha`
with evidence `ha` of `a`.

*)

intro a ha hna
apply (negation elimination) a hna ha
qed

theorem (of negation)


(∀a b.not a → a → b)

intro a b hna ha
apply (of false) b
apply (negation elimination) a hna ha
qed

theorem (negation of)


(∀a b.a → not a → b)

intro a b ha hna
apply (of false) b
apply (negation elimination) a hna ha
qed

theorem (converse law)

(∀a b.(a → b) → not b → not a)

(*

Had we `a`, we could show `b`, contradicting `not b`.
The converse law holds but its reverse doesn't.

Here, the directive `push` is used to add
an antecedent to the goal.

*)

intro a b hab hnb
-- show `not a` by concluding `false` from `a`
apply (negation introduction) a
intro ha -- had we `a`,
push hab ha -- we could show `b`,
apply (negation elimination) b hnb -- contradicting `not b`
qed

theorem (double converse law)

(∀a b.(not a → not b) → b → not (not a))

(*

We can't show `a` from these but we can show
`not (not a)`.

*)

intro a b hab hnb
apply (negation introduction) (not a)
intro hna
push hnb
apply (negation elimination) b
apply hab hna
qed

theorem (double negation introduction)

(∀a.a → not (not a))

(*

Double negation is the statement that
something can't be negated. We're going to call
that irrefutability later and use it to elaborate on
the structures of other logics.

If we've concluded something then it so happens we
also can't negate that thing.

`negation introduction` gives us a single negation
and asks us to prove false.

*)

intro a ha
apply (negation introduction) (not a)
apply (false of negation) a ha
qed

theorem (triple negation collapse)

(∀a.not (not (not a)) → not a)

(*

This tells us that the phrase "not irrefutable" might
be indistinct from negation. In a specific way, it tells
us there are only three truth values.

The proof is to obtain the goal via `a → not (not a)`
by `(converse law)` and `(double negation introduction)`.

*)

intro a
apply (converse law) a (not (not a))
apply (double negation introduction) a
qed

theorem (negated implication)

(∀a b.not (a → b) → not b)

(*

If the the rooster's crow doesn't imply the
sun rises then, oddly enough, the sun doesn't rise,
since, if the sun did rise, that would be implied by
the rooster's crow.

*)

intro a b
apply (converse law) b (a -> b)
apply (left of two) b a
qed

theorem (negative implication symmetry)

(∀a b.(a → not b) → b → not a)

(*

Commute a negative implication.
This similar proposition is not provable:

∀a b.(not a → b) → not b → a

*)

intro a b h hb
apply (negation introduction) a
intro ha
push hb
apply (negation elimination) b
apply h ha
qed

theorem (negative contradiction)

(∀x.(x → not x) → not x)

(*

Our first argument from contradiction. If `x`
would imply `not x`, then `x` is negated.

*)

intro x hf
apply (negation introduction) x
intro hx
apply (false of negation) x hx
apply hf hx
qed

theorem (double negative contradiction)

(∀x.(not x → x) → not (not x))

(*

We cannot prove something by contradiction unless
it implies a negation. Instead, We can prove a double
negation by proving that a negation would
lead to a contradiction.

*)

intro x hf
apply (negation introduction) (not x)
intro hnx
apply (negation elimination) x hnx
apply hf hnx
qed

title: 035 Equality
text:
035 Equality

(*

We introduce `eq`, the equality connective.

Equality is often distinct from biconditional,
but this logic cannot distinguish propositions
from individuals, so equality would be
indistinguishable from the biconditional.

Since to include of a distinct biconditional
would add no detail, we don't.

*)

declare eq

axiom (equality introduction)

(∀a b.(a → b) → (b → a) → eq a b)

axiom (equality elimination)

(∀a b.eq a b → ∀c.((a → b) → (b → a) → c) → c)

schema p
axiom (congruent argument)

(∀a b.eq a b → eq (p a) (p b))

schema f g
axiom (congruent function)

(eq f g → ∀a.eq (f a) (g a))

theorem (reverse equality introduction)

(∀a b.(a → b) → (b → a) → eq b a)

intro a b hab hba
apply (equality introduction) b a hba hab
qed

theorem (equality left)

(∀a b.eq a b → a → b)

intro a b hbc ha
apply (equality elimination) a b hbc b
intro hab hba
apply hab ha
qed

theorem (equality right)

(∀a b.eq a b → b → a)

intro a b hbc hb
apply (equality elimination) a b hbc a
intro hab hba
apply hba hb
qed

theorem (equality reflexive)

(∀a.eq a a)

intro a
push (implication reflexive) a
intro ha
apply (equality introduction) a a ha ha
qed

theorem (equality symmetric)

(∀a b.eq a b → eq b a)

intro a b hab
apply (equality elimination) a b hab (eq b a)
apply (reverse equality introduction) a b
qed

theorem (equality transitive)

(∀a b c.eq a b → eq b c → eq a c)

intro a b c hab hbc
apply (equality elimination) a b hab (eq a c)
intro iab iba
apply (equality elimination) b c hbc (eq a c)
intro ibc icb
apply (equality introduction) a c
intro ha
apply ibc
apply iab ha
intro hc
apply iba
apply icb hc
qed

schema p
theorem (left substitution)

(∀a b.eq a b → p a → p b)

intro a b he
apply (equality left) (p a) (p b)
apply (congruent argument) p a b he
qed

schema p
theorem (right substitution)

(∀a b.eq a b → p b → p a)

intro a b he
apply (equality left) (p b) (p a)
apply (congruent argument) p b a
apply (equality symmetric) a b he
qed

theorem (non equality non self)

(∀a.not (eq a (not a)))

intro a
apply (negation introduction) (eq a (not a))
intro hi
apply (equality elimination) a (not a) hi false
intro hana hnaa
push (negative contradiction) a hana
intro hna
apply (negation elimination) a hna
apply hnaa hna
qed


theorem (negative equality)

(∀a b.eq a b → eq (not a) (not b))

intro a b h
apply (equality elimination) a b h (eq (not a) (not b))
intro hab hba
apply (equality introduction) (not a) (not b)
apply (converse law) b a hba
apply (converse law) a b hab
qed

theorem (true equality left)

(∀a.a → eq true a)

intro a ha
apply (equality introduction) true a
intro ht
apply ha
intro ha'
apply (true introduction)
qed

theorem (true equality right)

(∀a.a → eq a true)

intro a ha
apply (equality introduction) a true
intro ha'
apply (true introduction)
intro ht
apply ha
qed

theorem (false equality left)

(∀a.not a → eq false a)

intro a hna
apply (equality introduction) false a
apply (of false) a
apply (negation elimination) a hna
qed

theorem (false equality right)

(∀a.not a → eq a false)

intro a hna
apply (equality introduction) a false
apply (negation elimination) a hna
apply (of false) a
qed

-- schema p
-- theorem (universal equality)

-- (∀a.(p a → ∀x.p x) → eq (∀x.p x) a)

-- intro a f
-- apply (equality introduction) (∀x.p x) a
-- qed

title: 040 Conjunction
text:
040 Conjunction

(*

We introduce `and`, the conjunction connective.

*)

declare and

(*

The conjunction connective is perhaps the most intuitive
of our logical connectives. In intuitionistic logic,
when we say "A and B" (written as A ∧ B), we mean we have
*both* of the following:

- A constructive proof of A
- A constructive proof of B

For example, to prove "the number 6 is even AND
greater than 5", we must:

Demonstrate that 6 = 2k for some integer k
(specifically, k = 3) Show that 6 > 5 through
direct comparison.

*)

axiom (conjunction definition)

(∀a b.eq (and a b) (∀c.(a → b → c) → c))

(*

A conjunction proves something if its parts prove
that together.

*)

theorem (conjunction introduction)

(∀a b.a → b → and a b)

intro a b ha hb
push (conjunction definition) a b
intro hc
apply (equality elimination) (and a b) (∀c.(a → b → c) → c) hc (and a b)
intro hcl hcr
apply hcr
intro c habc
apply habc ha hb
qed

theorem (reverse conjunction introduction)

(∀a b.a -> b -> and b a)

(*

We'll use this a few times to make some proofs two
steps shorter.

It's also an opportunity to use `implication swap`.

*)

intro a b
apply (implication swap) b a (and b a) -- `a → b → and b a`
apply (conjunction introduction) b a -- `b → a → and b a`
qed

theorem (conjunction elimination)

(∀a b.and a b → (∀c.(a → b → c) → c))

intro a b hc
push (conjunction definition) a b
intro hb
apply (equality elimination) (and a b) (∀c.(a → b → c) → c) hb (∀c.(a → b → c) → c)
intro hbl hbr
apply hbl hc
qed

theorem (left conjunction elimination)

(∀a b.and a b → a)

(*

We can obtain the left side of a conjunction.
We use `(conjunction elimination)` to convert
the conjuncts into antecedents.

*)

intro a b hc
apply (conjunction elimination) a b hc a

(*

a b
hc : and a b
⊢ a → b → a

Notice we had to mention the current goal
proposition `a` where specializing `conjunction elimination`.

At this point the goal is just (left of two).

*)

apply (left of two) a b
qed

theorem (right conjunction elimination)

(∀a b.and a b → b)

(*

We can obtain the right side of a conjunction.

*)

intro a b hc
apply (conjunction elimination) a b hc b
apply (right of two) a b
qed

theorem (self conjunction elimination)

(∀a.and a a → a)

(*

Slightly simpler to use this compared to
`left conjunction elimination` in some cases.

*)

intro a hc
apply (left conjunction elimination) a a hc
qed

theorem (conjunction symmetric)

(∀a b.and a b → and b a)

(*

We can exchange the conjuncts of `and`. If it's
tuesday and it's raining then it's raining and
it's tuesday.

*)

intro a b hab
apply (conjunction elimination) a b hab (and b a)
apply (reverse conjunction introduction) a b
qed

theorem (left non conjunction introduction)

(∀a b.not a → not (and a b))

(*

Conjunctions are false when the left conjunct is false.
If I were to ask you "are both options okay?" and
the first isn't, you'd tell me "no".

*)

intro a b hna
apply (converse law) (and a b) a
apply (left conjunction elimination) a b
apply hna
qed

theorem (right non conjunction introduction)

(∀a b.not b → not (and a b))

(*

You'd also tell me no when the second option isn't okay.

*)

intro a b hnb
apply (converse law) (and a b) b
apply (right conjunction elimination) a b
apply hnb
qed

theorem (non conjunction introduction)

(∀a b.
  (
    (not a → not (and a b)) →
    (not b → not (and a b)) →
    not (and a b)) →
  not (and a b))

intro a b f
apply f
apply (left non conjunction introduction) a b
apply (right non conjunction introduction) a b
qed

theorem (left non conjunction elimination)

(∀a b.a → not (and a b) → not b)

(*

Sometimes two things can't be true. If you know
that the sun is up then you can also know
it's not night if you know those don't coincide.

*)

intro a b ha hnc
apply (converse law) b (and a b)
apply (conjunction introduction) a b ha
apply hnc
qed

theorem (right non conjunction elimination)

(∀a b.b → not (and a b) → not a)

(*

Commutation of the previous.

*)

intro a b hb hnc
apply (converse law) a (and a b)
apply (reverse conjunction introduction) b a hb
apply hnc
qed

theorem (non conjunction of non self)

(∀a.not (and a (not a)))

(*

Conjunction with negation of self leads to a contradiction.

*)

intro a
apply (negation introduction) (and a (not a))
intro hi
apply (conjunction elimination) a (not a) hi false
apply (false of negation) a
qed

title: 050 Disjunction
text:
050 Disjunction

(*

We introduce `or`, the disjunction connective.

*)

declare or

(*

The disjunction connective is dual (in a specific way)
to the conjunction connective. In intuitionistic logic,
when we say "A or B" (written as A ∨ B), we mean we have
*at least one* of the following:

- A constructive proof of A
- A constructive proof of B

This differs from classical logic where we might
prove A ∨ B by showing that ¬(¬A ∧ ¬B). In
intuitionistic logic, such indirect proofs are
not accepted - we need explicit construction.

*)

axiom (disjunction introduction)

(∀a b.((a → or a b) → (b → or a b) → or a b) → or a b)

(*

Disjunction is a proposition of one of two others.
We may have proof of a disjunction if we have proof
of either disjunct.

*)

axiom (disjunction elimination)

(∀a b.or a b → ∀c.(a → c) → (b → c) → c)

(*

A disjunction proves something if one of its
parts prove that together.

*)

theorem (left disjunction introduction)

(∀a b.a → or a b)

(*

Since the disjunction is true when either
disjunct is true, we can prove a disjunction
with proof of just one.

*)

intro a b ha
apply (disjunction introduction) a b
intro l r
apply l ha
qed

theorem (right disjunction introduction)

(∀a b.b → or a b)

intro a b hb
apply (disjunction introduction) a b
intro l r
apply r hb
qed

theorem (self disjunction introduction)

(∀a.a → or a a)

(*

Identity is self-disjunction.

*)

intro a ha
apply (left disjunction introduction) a a ha
qed

theorem (self disjunction elimination)

(∀a.or a a → a)

(*

Self-disjunction is identity.

*)

intro a hd
apply (disjunction elimination) a a hd a
apply (implication reflexive) a
apply (implication reflexive) a
qed

theorem (self disjunction iff)

(∀a.eq (or a a) a)

intro a
apply (equality introduction) (or a a) a
apply (self disjunction elimination) a
apply (self disjunction introduction) a
qed

theorem (disjunction symmetric)

(∀a b.or a b → or b a)

(*

Disjunction, like conjunction, is symmetric.

*)

intro a b hab
apply (disjunction introduction) b a
intro ob oa
apply (disjunction elimination) a b hab (or b a) oa ob
qed

theorem (disjunction commutative)

(∀a b.eq (or a b) (or b a))

intro a b
apply (equality introduction) (or a b) (or b a)
apply (disjunction symmetric) a b
apply (disjunction symmetric) b a
qed

theorem (left disjunction elimination) 

(∀a b.not b → or a b → a)

(*

You can obtain proof of the left disjunct if you
can negate the right disjunct.

*)

intro a b hnb hd
apply (disjunction elimination) a b hd a
apply (implication reflexive) a
intro hb
apply (of false) a
apply (negation elimination) b hnb hb
qed

theorem (right disjunction elimination)

(∀a b.not a → or a b → b)

(*

You can obtain proof of the right disjunct if you
can negate the left disjunct.

*)

intro a b hna hd
apply (disjunction elimination) a b hd b
intro ha
apply (of false) b
apply (negation elimination) a hna ha
apply (implication reflexive) b
qed

theorem (left disjunction elimination eq)

(∀a b.not b → eq (or a b) a)

(*

You can obtain proof of the right disjunct if you
can negate the left disjunct.

*)

intro a b hnb
apply (equality introduction) (or a b) a
apply (left disjunction elimination) a b hnb
apply (left disjunction introduction) a b
qed

theorem (right disjunction elimination iff)

(∀a b.not a → eq (or a b) b)

(*

You can obtain proof of the right disjunct if you
can negate the left disjunct.

*)

intro a b hna
apply (equality introduction) (or a b) b
apply (right disjunction elimination) a b hna
apply (right disjunction introduction) a b
qed

theorem (non disjunction introduction)

(∀a b.not a → not b → not (or a b))

(*

You can negate a disjunction if you can negate
both disjuncts.

*)

intro a b hna hnb
apply (negation introduction) (or a b)
intro hd
apply (disjunction elimination) a b hd false
apply (negation elimination) a hna
apply (negation elimination) b hnb
qed

theorem (left non disjunction elimination)

(∀a b.not (or a b) → not b)

intro a b hnd
apply (negation introduction) b
intro hnb
apply (negation elimination) (or a b) hnd
apply (right disjunction introduction) a b hnb
qed

theorem (right non disjunction elimination)

(∀a b.not (or a b) → not a)

intro a b hnd
apply (negation introduction) a
intro hna
apply (negation elimination) (or a b) hnd
apply (left disjunction introduction) a b hna
qed

theorem (non disjunction elimination)

(∀a b.not (or a b) → ∀c.(not a -> not b -> c) -> c)

intro a b hnd c f
apply f
apply (right non disjunction elimination) a b hnd
apply (left non disjunction elimination) a b hnd
qed

title: 060 DeMorgan Laws
text:
060 DeMorgan Laws

(*

Classical logic has four DeMorgan laws, but our
logic can only prove three. The fourth law will
appear later with a stipulation that involves
double negation.

*)

theorem (negative conjunction)

(∀a b.not (or a b) → and (not a) (not b))

intro a b hd
apply (non disjunction elimination) a b hd (and (not a) (not b))
apply (conjunction introduction) (not a) (not b)
qed

theorem (non disjunction)

(∀a b.and (not a) (not b) → not (or a b))

intro a b hc
apply (conjunction elimination) (not a) (not b) hc (not (or a b))
apply (non disjunction introduction) a b
qed

theorem (non conjunction)

(∀a b.or (not a) (not b) → not (and a b))

(*

This is the one whose reverse isn't provable.

*)

intro a b hd
apply (non conjunction introduction) a b
apply (disjunction elimination) (not a) (not b) hd (not (and a b))
qed

title: 070 Conditional
text:
070 Conditional

declare if

axiom (conditional definition)

(∀c a b.eq (if c a b) (∀e.(c -> a -> e) -> (not c -> b -> e) -> e))

theorem (true conditional)

(∀a b.eq (if true a b) a)

intro a b
push (conditional definition) true a b
intro hc
apply (equality transitive) (if true a b) (∀e.(true → a → e) → (not true → b → e) → e) a hc
apply (equality introduction) (∀e.(true → a → e) → (not true → b → e) → e) a
intro f
apply f a
intro ht
apply (implication reflexive) a
intro hf hb
apply (of false) a
apply (non true) hf
intro ha
intro e l r
apply l (true introduction) ha
qed

theorem (false conditional)

(∀a b.eq (if false a b) b)

intro a b
push (conditional definition) false a b
intro hc
apply (equality transitive) (if false a b) (∀e.(false → a → e) → (not false → b → e) → e) b hc
apply (equality introduction) (∀e.(false → a → e) → (not false → b → e) → e) b
intro f
apply f b
intro hf ha
apply (of false) b hf
intro ht
apply (implication reflexive) b
intro hb
intro e l r
apply r (non false) hb
qed

title: 100 Sets
text:
100 Sets

(*

We introduce the notion of a set defined according
to the axioms of ZF.

`set a` just says that `a` is a set.
We use this to ensure that sets are only
built from other sets, and not from other
propositions.

`elem e s` says `e` is an element of `s.
This relation is arbitrary for opaque
sets and impredicatively defined for sets
constructed from the axioms.

`empty` is the empty set, the set for which
every proposition is not an element.

*)

declare set elem subset empty

axiom (empty definition)

(and (set empty)
  (∀e.not (elem e empty)))

(*

We cannot prove
the existence of an empty set from the ZF axioms,
but we're going to postulate it.

*)

theorem (empty set)

(set empty)

apply (left conjunction elimination) (set empty) (∀e.not (elem e empty)) (empty definition)
qed

theorem (empty elements)

(∀e.not (elem e empty))

apply (right conjunction elimination) (set empty) (∀e.not (elem e empty)) (empty definition)
qed

axiom (subset definition)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  iff (subset a b) (
  ∀e.elem e a → elem e b))

theorem (subset introduction)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  (∀e.elem e a → elem e b) →
  subset a b)

intro a b hsa hsb
push (subset definition) a b hsa hsb
apply (biconditional right) (subset a b) (∀e.elem e a → elem e b)
qed

theorem (subset elimination)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  subset a b →
  (∀e.elem e a → elem e b))

intro a b hsa hsb
push (subset definition) a b hsa hsb
apply (biconditional left) (subset a b) (∀e.elem e a → elem e b)
qed

axiom (set extensionality)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  iff (eq a b) (
  ∀e.iff (elem e a) (elem e b)))

(*

If two sets have all the same elements, then
they are equal.

*)

declare comprehension

schema p 
axiom (set comprehension)

(∀a.
  set a →
  and (set (comprehension p a)) (
  ∀e.iff (elem e (comprehension p a)) (
  and (elem e a) (p e))))

(*

Construct a subset by comprehension.

*)

declare pair

axiom (set pairing)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  and (set (pair a b)) (
  ∀e.iff (elem e (pair a b)) (
  or (eq e a) (eq e b))))

(*

Construct a pair of two sets.

*)

declare union

axiom (set union)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  and (set (union a b)) (
  ∀e.iff (elem e (union a b)) (
  or (elem e a) (elem e b))))

(*

Construct the union of two sets.

*)

declare replacement

schema p
axiom (set replacement)

(∀a.
  set a →
  and (set (replacement p a)) (
  ∀e.iff (elem e a) (
  elem (p e) (replacement p a))))

(*

Construct the image of a set under a function.

*)

theorem (set equality introduction)

(∀a b.set a → set b → (∀c.iff (elem c a) (elem c b)) → eq a b)

intro a b hsa hsb hi
push (set extensionality) a b hsa hsb
intro hc
apply (biconditional right) (eq a b) (∀e.iff (elem e a) (elem e b)) hc hi
qed

theorem (set equality elimination)

(∀a b.set a → set b → eq a b → (∀c.iff (elem c a) (elem c b)))

intro a b hsa hsb he
push (set extensionality) a b hsa hsb
intro hc
apply (biconditional left) (eq a b) (∀e.iff (elem e a) (elem e b)) hc he
qed

theorem (union set)

(∀a b.set a → set b → set (union a b))

intro a b hsa hsb
push (set union) a b hsa hsb
intro hc
apply (left conjunction elimination) (set (union a b)) (∀e.iff (elem e (union a b)) (or (elem e a) (elem e b))) hc
qed

theorem (union elements)

(∀a b.
  set a →
  set b →
  ∀e.iff (elem e (union a b)) (
  or (elem e a) (elem e b)))

intro a b hsa hsb
push (set union) a b hsa hsb
intro hc
apply (right conjunction elimination) (set (union a b)) (∀e.iff (elem e (union a b)) (or (elem e a) (elem e b))) hc
qed

theorem (union symmetric)

(∀a b.set a → set b → eq (union a b) (union b a))

intro a b hsa hsb
apply (biconditional right) (eq (union a b) (union b a)) (∀e.iff (elem e (union a b)) (elem e (union b a)))
apply (set extensionality) (union a b) (union b a)
apply (union set) a b hsa hsb
apply (union set) b a hsb hsa
intro e
apply (biconditional transitive) (elem e (union a b)) (or (elem e a) (elem e b)) (elem e (union b a))
apply (union elements) a b hsa hsb e
apply (biconditional transitive) (or (elem e a) (elem e b)) (or (elem e b) (elem e a)) (elem e (union b a))
apply (disjunction commutative) (elem e a) (elem e b)
apply (biconditional symmetric) (elem e (union b a)) (or (elem e b) (elem e a))
apply (union elements) b a hsb hsa e
qed

theorem (empty union)

(∀a.
  set a →
  eq (union empty a) a)

intro a hsa
apply (set equality introduction) (union empty a) a
apply (union set) empty a (empty set) hsa
apply hsa
intro e
apply (biconditional transitive) (elem e (union empty a)) (or (elem e empty) (elem e a)) (elem e a)
apply (union elements) empty a (empty set) hsa e
apply (right disjunction elimination iff) (elem e empty) (elem e a)
apply (empty elements) e
qed

theorem (union empty)

(∀a.
  set a →
  eq (union a empty) a)

intro a hsa
push (union symmetric) a empty hsa (empty set)
intro ha
push (empty union) a hsa
apply (equality transitive) (union a empty) (union empty a) a ha
qed

theorem (empty subset)

(∀a.
  set a →
  subset empty a)

intro a hsa
apply (subset introduction) empty a (empty set) hsa
intro e
apply (of negation) (elem e empty) (elem e a)
apply (empty elements) e
qed

title: 200 Natural Numbers
text:
200 Natural Numbers

(*

We introduce the natural numbers.

We use an approach that doesn't involve set
theory because ZF can't actually construct
the nats anyway.

`nat a` is the proposition that `a` is a
natural number. It's used as a barrier to
ensure the axioms do not apply to propositions
other than natural numbers.

`zero` and `succ` are the two constructors
of `nat`.

*)

declare nat zero succ

axiom (natural zero)

(nat zero)

(*

`zero` is a natural number.

*)

axiom (natural successor)

(∀a.nat a → nat (succ a))

(*

If `n` is a natural number, then `succ n`
is also a natural number.

*)

axiom (natural no confusion)

(∀a.nat a → not (eq zero (succ a)))

(*

No natural number's successor is zero.

*)

axiom (successor injective)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (succ a) (succ b) → eq a b)

(*

The successor function is injective.

*)

schema p
axiom (natural induction)

(p zero → (∀n.nat n → p n → p (succ n)) → ∀n.nat n → p n)

(*

We introduce `one`.

*)

declare one

axiom (one definition)

(eq one (succ zero))

(*

One is the successor of zero.

*)

theorem (natural one)

(nat one)

(*

One is a natural number.

*)

apply (right substitution) nat one (succ zero) (one definition)
apply (natural successor) zero (natural zero)
qed

(*

We introduce `add`, the addition operation.

*)

declare add

axiom (addition definition)

(∀a b.
  nat a →
  nat b →
  eq (add a b) (
  if (eq zero b) a (
  ∀c.nat c →
  eq b (succ c) →
  succ (add a c))))

(*

Addition is defined for two operands such that
it is equal to the first when the second is equal
to zero. When the second is `succ c` the addition
is `succ (add a c)`.

We use this single definition axiom to obtain the
usual piecwise axioms as theorems.

*)

theorem (zero addition right)

(∀a.nat a → eq (add a zero) a)

(*

The usual zero part of Peano addition.

*)

intro a hna
apply (equality transitive) (add a zero) (if (eq zero zero) a ∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → succ (add a c)) a
apply (addition definition) a zero hna (natural zero)
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (if x a ∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → succ (add a c)) a) (eq zero zero) true
apply (true equality right) (eq zero zero)
apply (equality reflexive) zero
apply (true conditional) a (∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → succ (add a c))
qed

theorem (successor addition right)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (add a (succ b)) (succ (add a b)))

(*

The usual successor part of Peano addition.

*)

intro a b hna hnb
apply (equality transitive) (add a (succ b)) (if (eq zero (succ b)) a ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c)) (succ (add a b))
apply (addition definition) a (succ b) hna
apply (natural successor) b hnb
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (if x a ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c)) (succ (add a b))) (eq zero (succ b)) false
apply (false equality right) (eq zero (succ b))
apply (natural no confusion) b hnb
apply (equality transitive) (if false a ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c)) (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c)) (succ (add a b))
apply (false conditional) a (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c))
apply (equality introduction) (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → succ (add a c)) (succ (add a b))
intro hf
apply hf b hnb
apply (equality reflexive) (succ b)
intro ha c hnc he
apply (left substitution) (∀x.succ (add a x)) b c
apply (successor injective) b c hnb hnc he
apply ha
qed

theorem (addition natural)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → nat (add a b))

(*

Naturals are closed under addition.

This is our first usage of the directive `with`.
It's the simplest directive. `with b` changes the
goal from `E` to `∀b.E` since if we can prove E
for all `b` then we can prove `E`.

It's necessary here to set the goal up for induction.

*)

intro a b hna
with b
apply (natural induction) (∀b.nat (add a b))
apply (right substitution) nat (add a zero) a
apply (zero addition right) a hna
apply hna
intro n hnn hi
apply (right substitution) nat (add a (succ n)) (succ (add a n))
apply (successor addition right) a n hna hnn
apply (natural successor) (add a n) hi
qed

theorem (zero addition left)

(∀a.nat a → eq (add zero a) a)

apply (natural induction) (∀a.eq (add zero a) a)
apply (zero addition right) zero (natural zero)
intro n hnn hi
apply (left substitution) (∀x.eq (add zero (succ n)) (succ x)) (add zero n) n hi
apply (successor addition right) zero n (natural zero) hnn
qed

theorem (successor addition left)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (add (succ a) b) (succ (add a b)))

intro a b hna
with b
apply (natural induction) (∀b.eq (add (succ a) b) (succ (add a b)))
apply (equality transitive) (add (succ a) zero) (succ a) (succ (add a zero))
apply (zero addition right) (succ a)
apply (natural successor) a hna
apply (equality symmetric) (succ (add a zero)) (succ a)
apply (congruent argument) succ (add a zero) a
apply (zero addition right) a hna
intro n hnn hi
apply (equality transitive) (add (succ a) (succ n)) (succ (add (succ a) n)) (succ (add a (succ n)))
apply (successor addition right) (succ a) n
apply (natural successor) a hna
apply hnn
apply (congruent argument) succ (add (succ a) n) (add a (succ n))
apply (equality transitive) (add (succ a) n) (succ (add a n)) (add a (succ n)) hi
apply (equality symmetric) (add a (succ n)) (succ (add a n))
apply (successor addition right) a n hna hnn
qed

theorem (addition commutative)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (add a b) (add b a))

intro a b hna
with b
apply (natural induction) (∀b.eq (add a b) (add b a))
apply (equality transitive) (add a zero) a (add zero a)
apply (zero addition right) a hna
apply (equality symmetric) (add zero a) a
apply (zero addition left) a hna
intro n hnn hi
apply (equality transitive) (add a (succ n)) (succ (add a n)) (add (succ n) a)
apply (successor addition right) a n hna hnn
apply (equality transitive) (succ (add a n)) (succ (add n a)) (add (succ n) a)
apply (congruent argument) succ (add a n) (add n a) hi
apply (equality symmetric) (add (succ n) a) (succ (add n a))
apply (successor addition left) n a hnn hna
qed

theorem (unit addition right)

(∀a.nat a → eq (add a one) (succ a))

intro a hna
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (add a x) (succ a)) one (succ zero) (one definition)
apply (equality transitive) (add a (succ zero)) (succ (add a zero)) (succ a)
apply (successor addition right) a zero hna (natural zero)
apply (congruent argument) succ (add a zero) a
apply (zero addition right) a hna
qed

theorem (unit addition left)

(∀a.nat a → eq (add one a) (succ a))

intro a hna
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (add x a) (succ a)) one (succ zero) (one definition)
apply (equality transitive) (add (succ zero) a) (succ (add zero a)) (succ a)
apply (successor addition left) zero a (natural zero) hna
apply (congruent argument) succ (add zero a) a
apply (zero addition left) a hna
qed

declare mul

axiom (multiplication definition)

(∀a b.
  nat a →
  nat b →
  eq (mul a b) (
  if (eq zero b) zero (
  ∀c.nat c →
  eq b (succ c) →
  add a (mul a c))))

theorem (zero multiplication right)

(∀a.nat a → eq (mul a zero) zero)

intro a hna
apply (equality transitive) (mul a zero) (if (eq zero zero) zero ∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) zero
apply (multiplication definition) a zero hna (natural zero)
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (if x zero ∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) zero) (eq zero zero) true
apply (true equality right) (eq zero zero)
apply (equality reflexive) zero
apply (true conditional) zero (∀c.nat c → eq zero (succ c) → add a (mul a c))
qed

theorem (successor multiplication right)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (mul a (succ b)) (add a (mul a b)))


intro a b hna hnb
apply (equality transitive) (mul a (succ b)) (if (eq zero (succ b)) zero ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) (add a (mul a b))
apply (multiplication definition) a (succ b) hna
apply (natural successor) b hnb
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (if x zero ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) (add a (mul a b))) (eq zero (succ b)) false
apply (false equality right) (eq zero (succ b))
apply (natural no confusion) b hnb
apply (equality transitive) (if false zero ∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) (add a (mul a b))
apply (false conditional) zero (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c))
apply (equality introduction) (∀c.nat c → eq (succ b) (succ c) → add a (mul a c)) (add a (mul a b))
intro hf
apply hf b hnb
apply (equality reflexive) (succ b)
intro ha c hnc he
apply (left substitution) (∀x.add a (mul a x)) b c
apply (successor injective) b c hnb hnc he
apply ha
qed

theorem (multiplication natural)

(∀a b.nat a → nat b → nat (mul a b))

(*

Naturals are closed under multiplication.

*)

intro a b hna
with b
apply (natural induction) (∀b.nat (mul a b))
apply (right substitution) nat (mul a zero) zero
apply (zero multiplication right) a hna
apply (natural zero)
intro n hnn hi
apply (right substitution) nat (mul a (succ n)) (add a (mul a n))
apply (successor multiplication right) a n hna hnn
apply (addition natural) a (mul a n) hna hi
qed

theorem (unit multiplication right)

(∀a.nat a → eq (mul a one) a)

intro a hna
apply (right substitution) (∀x.eq (mul a x) a) one (succ zero) (one definition)
apply (equality transitive) (mul a (succ zero)) (add a (mul a zero)) a
apply (successor multiplication right) a zero hna (natural zero)
apply (equality transitive) (add a (mul a zero)) (add a zero) a
apply (congruent argument) (add a) (mul a zero) zero
apply (zero multiplication right) a hna
apply (zero addition right) a hna
qed

theorem (zero multiplication left)

(∀a.nat a → eq (mul zero a) zero)

apply (natural induction) (∀a.eq (mul zero a) zero)
apply (zero multiplication right) zero (natural zero)
intro n hnn hi
apply (equality transitive) (mul zero (succ n)) (add zero (mul zero n)) zero
apply (successor multiplication right) zero n (natural zero) hnn
apply (equality transitive) (add zero (mul zero n)) (mul zero n) zero
apply (zero addition left) (mul zero n)
apply (multiplication natural) zero n (natural zero) hnn
apply hi
qed

theorem (unit multiplication left)

(∀a.nat a → eq (mul one a) a)

apply (natural induction) (∀a.eq (mul one a) a)
apply (zero multiplication right) one (natural one)
intro n hnn hi
apply (equality transitive) (mul one (succ n)) (add one (mul one n)) (succ n)
apply (successor multiplication right) one n (natural one) hnn
apply (equality transitive) (add one (mul one n)) (succ (mul one n)) (succ n)
apply (unit addition left) (mul one n)
apply (multiplication natural) one n (natural one) hnn
apply (congruent argument) succ (mul one n) n hi
qed

-- theorem (succ mul)

-- (∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (mul (succ a) b) (add b (mul a b)))

-- intro a b hna
-- with b
-- apply (natural induction) (∀b.eq (mul (succ a) b) (add b (mul a b)))

-- apply (zero addition left) (mul a zero)
-- apply (multiplication natural) a zero hna (natural zero)
-- apply (zero multiplication right) a hna
-- intro n hnn hi
-- -- apply (equality transitive) (mul (succ a) (succ n)) (add (succ n) (mul a (succ n)))
-- qed

-- (∀a b.nat a → nat b → eq (mul a b) (mul b a))

-- intro a b hna

-- apply (natural induction) (∀b.eq (mul a b) (mul b a))
-- apply (equality transitive) (mul a zero) zero (mul zero a)
-- apply (zero multiplication right) a hna
-- apply (equality symmetric) (mul zero a) zero

title: 300 Real Numbers
text:
300 Real Numbers

declare neg sub div gt lt ge le positive negative nonzero abs

declare real

axiom (zero real)

(real zero)

axiom (one real)

(real one)

axiom (positive definition)

(∀a.real a → eq (positive a) (lt zero a))

axiom (one positive)

(positive one)

axiom (one nonzero)

(nonzero one)

axiom (real addition commutative)

(∀a b.real a → real b → eq (add a b) (add b a))

axiom (real addition associative)

(∀a b c.real a → real b → real c → eq (add a (add b c)) (add (add a b) c))

axiom (lt transitive)

(∀a b c.real a → real b → real c → lt a b → lt b c → lt a c)

axiom (self division)

(∀a b c.real a → nonzero a → eq (div a a) one)

axiom (division real)

(∀a b.real a → real b → nonzero b → real (div a b))

title: 350 Limits
text:
350 Limits

declare limit

schema f
axiom (limit definition)

(∀a.
  real a →
  ∀L.real L →
  (
    ∀ε.real ε →
    positive ε →
    ∃δ.and (real δ) (
    and (positive δ) (
    ∀x.real x →
    real (f x) →
    lt (abs (sub x a)) δ →
    lt (abs (sub (f x) L)) ε))) →
